angle: Prompt Engineering Didn't Die, It Grew Up: The Case for Context Engineering
audience: Developer- and AI-engineering-focused podcasts and technical publications. Their listeners build LLM applications and agents and are working out how to get from a good demo to a reliable production system.

talking_points.text: Thomas argues that prompt engineering didn't die; it evolved into the broader practice of context engineering.
In his view, clever prompts produce impressive demos, but well-structured context produces production-ready systems.
He argues that reliable autonomous agents come from better context architecture, not better prompts.
The foundation of context engineering, he says, is treating documentation as machine-readable context rather than only as reference material for humans.
He sees the 2025 shift from vibes-based AI development to systematic context management as a lasting change, not a passing trend.
For organizations, he frames the decision as how quickly to build context-engineering capability, not whether to invest in it.
He brings a practitioner's view because he writes production code daily and ships AI-powered systems using Claude, GPT-4, and agentic coding pipelines.

angle: The Model Usually Works: Why AI Initiatives Really Fail and What to Do Instead
audience: Business, executive-leadership, and digital-transformation shows and outlets. Their audience of CEOs, CIOs, and senior decision-makers owns AI budgets and needs to know why so many initiatives stall.

talking_points.text: Thomas says that in every failed AI project he has audited, the root cause was never the algorithm but data quality, unclear objectives, or a lack of organizational readiness.
He argues that most organizations overestimate their data readiness and should budget 60–70% of project effort for data work.
In his view, the model usually works, and most AI initiatives quietly die on adoption and trust.
He says the best AI projects start with a business problem, not with the goal of using AI, and should be pursued only if they can deliver at least a 10x improvement in a key metric.

He argues that general executive support isn't enough: AI needs a senior owner who will fight for budget when the first pilot disappoints, and transformation lands only when a single accountable owner drives it.
He says enterprises often stick to low-risk copilot tools to avoid model-risk governance.
He favors a 90-day pilot with clear success metrics over a 12-month roadmap with vague outcomes, and deliberate maturity-building over fragile quick fixes.
His bottom line is that organizations winning with AI have the clearest strategy and the discipline to execute it, not necessarily the most sophisticated technology.

angle: The Builder Executive: Leading AI-Augmented Engineering Teams from the Commit Level
audience: Engineering-leadership and CTO-focused podcasts and publications. Their audience of engineering managers, VPs, and CTOs is rethinking team structure, AI tooling, and how credit works when AI contributes to the work.

talking_points.text: Thomas argues that technology executives should stay hands-on builders, and he still writes production code daily in Python, TypeScript, and infrastructure-as-code.
He says good tech leadership means understanding what's happening at the commit level, not only setting strategy.
He builds teams that are people-first, globally distributed for 24/7 delivery, and AI-augmented with modern tooling.
He argues that requiring engineers to attribute work to AI backfires because they don't want their best contributions footnoted as 'cowritten by Claude.'
The fix that worked, he says, was crediting outcomes over tools: the responsible person owns the credit and the blame, however much AI helped.
His leadership approach puts results over process and relies on evidence-based decisions and right-sized solutions.
He aims to build technology organizations that don't just execute but compound, and he brings the same discipline and endurance mindset he applies to crossing finish lines.
